world_behind.title: Jacob's words, mostly unwritten
world_behind.text: Verse 1 mentions that Nephi can write only a few of his brother's words, a passing remark with consequences: Jacob preached for years and what survives is one sermon and a short book. The small plates are selective by necessity, and Nephi says so at the moment he begins his own conclusion.

world_behind.title: Baptism, six centuries early
world_behind.text: The chapter describes baptism by water, the Holy Ghost, and the formula of entering by a gate, before any of it exists as practice in Israel. Nephi grounds it on what he was shown in vision about the Lamb of God being baptized, which he had reported fifteen chapters into his first book.

world_behind.title: Three voices heard
world_behind.text: The Father speaks in verse 11, the Son in verses 12 and 14, and the Father again in verse 15. Nephi is quoting revelation given to him personally, and the passage is one of the record's few places where the two are heard in sequence about the same subject.

world_behind.title: A question asked of the audience
world_behind.text: Verse 6 stops the argument and asks the brethren directly why the Lamb was baptized, and verse 19 asks whether entering the gate finishes the matter. Both are answered immediately. Nephi is teaching in the manner of a man in a room, not writing an essay, and the questions mark where he expects resistance.

world_behind.title: The tongue of angels
world_behind.text: Verse 13 promises that the baptized may speak with the tongue of angels, and the next chapter will explain what that means in practical terms. Nephi introduces the phrase here without definition and answers the obvious question one page later. The arrangement is deliberate.

world_behind.title: Water first, then fire
world_behind.text: Verse 17 puts baptism by water before baptism by fire and the Holy Ghost, and verse 8 has the dove descending after the water. The order is stated twice and it is the record's settled sequence, which later writers assume without restating.

words.text: A legal verb: to give formal testimony before someone. The Lamb's baptism is described as witnessing unto the Father that he would be obedient, so the ordinance is treated as a sworn statement rather than as a cleansing. Verse 13 asks the same of everybody else, in the same word.

The one physical image in a chapter of procedure. The Holy Ghost descends in the form of a dove, and the record gives no interpretation of the bird. The detail sits between the baptism and the gate as the only thing in the sequence a person could have watched.

The word does two jobs in this chapter. It is Nephi's ordinary address to his hearers, "my beloved brethren" (v. 1), and he repeats it at nearly every turn until a reader stops hearing it. Then the Father speaks and uses it of one person, "my Beloved Son" (v. 11), and four verses later drops the noun: "the words of my Beloved are true and faithful" (v. 15). The chapter's most routine form of address turns out to be the Father's name for the Son.

cites.quote: the words of my Beloved are true and faithful

spans.text: the words of my Beloved are true and faithful

words.text: A remission is a release, the cancelling of something owed. Verse 17 does not say the sins are undone or forgotten; it says "a remission of your sins by fire and by the Holy Ghost" (v. 17) follows the water. What is described is a debt discharged by someone with standing to discharge it. The gospels use the word for what the blood of Christ is shed for (Matt. 26:28), and this record makes it the standard term for forgiveness received.

cites.quote: a remission of your sins by fire and by the Holy Ghost

spans.text: a remission of your sins by fire and by the Holy Ghost

words.text: A merit is something earned, a claim on reward. Nephi has just walked his hearers through everything the disciple does, repentance, baptism, following, and then says they came that far only with unshaken faith, "relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save" (v. 19). The earning sits on one side of that sentence and the reliance on the other. The noun belongs to Christ everywhere the record uses it, down to Moroni's closing instruction to rely "alone upon the merits of Christ" (Moro. 6:4); the word is not in the King James Bible at all.

cites.quote: relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save

spans.text: relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save

words.text: Not reading, studying, or pondering. The verb is about eating at length and with pleasure, and its object is the word of Christ. Placed between pressing forward and enduring to the end, it is the chapter's only image of enjoyment, and the chapter's practical instruction for how the enduring is fueled.

phrases.text: Named at the start and again in the last verse, which brackets the chapter. Everything between is the content: an example, a sequence, a gate, a path, and an end. The record uses the phrase afterward as a fixed term, and this chapter is what it points at.

The delight formula, first used in the psalm and then of Isaiah's words, now attached to plainness itself. Nephi gives the reason in the same verse: God speaks to men "according to their language, unto their understanding" (v. 3). Plainness is not his preference; it is described as God's method.

cites.quote: according to their language, unto their understanding

spans.text: according to their language, unto their understanding

phrases.term: How much more need have we, being unholy
phrases.text: The argument from the greater to the lesser. If a holy man was baptized, an unholy one has more need, not less. Nephi builds the whole case for baptism on one asymmetry, and the rhetorical force depends on granting the first premise, which he assumes his hearers already do.

phrases.term: He humbleth himself before the Father
phrases.text: The answer to the question verse 6 asks. Righteousness is fulfilled by a person submitting, and the verse specifies what the submission witnesses: obedience in keeping the commandments. The example is made of a posture.

Strait means narrow or tight, from the same root as the strait between two landmasses rather than from straight; paired with the narrowness of the gate, the two words say one thing twice. The Sermon on the Mount uses the same pair, that "strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life" (Matt. 7:14). Nephi has both, in reverse order, and attaches them to the baptism he has just described. The gate is not a metaphor for a decision here; it is an ordinance.

Three words, quoted as the Lord's, and the chapter's hinge. Verse 10 turns immediately to the consequence: following cannot be separated from keeping the commandments of the Father. Nephi does not treat discipleship as a feeling toward a person; he treats it as imitation.

Last in a run of qualifiers, three of them negative and this one positive, and it is the phrase the record keeps. Together they describe someone whose outward act and inward aim are the same thing. That is a harder standard than sincerity of feeling.

phrases.term: He that endureth to the end, the same shall be saved
phrases.text: The Father's own words, quoted, and the same promise the Lord makes in Matthew's gospel, that "he that endureth to the end shall be saved" (Matt. 10:22). In this chapter it functions as the answer to the question raised at verse 19, whether the gate is the end of the road.

phrases.term: If all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay
phrases.text: The chapter's structural surprise. Everything to this point has built a sequence that culminates in the gate; verse 19 asks whether that completes it and answers no. What follows is the record's most compact description of the life after conversion, and it is three verses long.

phrases.term: Press forward with a steadfastness in Christ
phrases.text: Steadfastness is firmness that does not shift, and here what does not shift is a direction. The verse names four things to carry: steadfastness, a perfect brightness of hope, love of God, and love of all men. Then two actions: press forward and feast. The sentence is the record's most quoted instruction for ordinary discipleship, and both its verbs are about continuing.

phrases.term: None other way nor name given under heaven
phrases.text: Peter tells a council that "there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). Nephi's version adds way to name, which matters in a chapter that has just described a path and a gate. The exclusivity claimed is about a route and a person together.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: Clearing his throat
verses.text: The record ends one thing and starts another inside three verses, and states a limit twice while doing it: "I cannot write but a few things," then "neither can I write but a few of the words of my brother Jacob." Verse 3 supplies a reason for the style that is a claim about God rather than about the writer: "for after this manner doth the Lord God work among the children of men... he speaketh unto men according to their language, unto their understanding." Plainness is defended at 2 Nephi 25:4 as the writer's own delight; here it is grounded in a divine method.

verses.label: v. 4–9
verses.title: The argument from the Lamb's baptism
verses.text: A holy man was baptized to fulfil all righteousness; therefore the unholy need it more. Verse 6 asks how it was fulfilled and verse 7 answers: humbling, witnessing, obedience. Then the dove, then the gate. The passage argues its case step by step, unusual for a chapter this often quoted for its conclusions.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: Three voices, one instruction
verses.text: The Lord's own words are quoted twice and the Father's once, and all three say the same thing in different registers: follow, repent and be baptized, and the Holy Ghost will be given. Nephi is reporting revelation, and the passage gets its authority from the revelation itself.

verses.label: v. 13
verses.title: The conditions, stated fully
verses.text: Full purpose of heart, no hypocrisy, no deception, real intent, repentance, and a witness to the Father. Then the promise of the Holy Ghost and the tongue of angels. It is the longest sentence in the chapter and the most demanding, and everything in it concerns sincerity rather than performance.

verses.label: v. 15–16
verses.title: The Father's word, and Nephi's inference
verses.text: The Father promises salvation to those who endure; Nephi then says he knows by this that a man who does not endure cannot be saved. The second sentence is his own reasoning from the first, and he says so, which is a useful example of how this record distinguishes revelation from conclusion.

verses.label: v. 17–18
verses.title: The gate, and what lies past it
verses.text: Baptism by water then by fire and the Holy Ghost, and then the path. Verse 18 lists what has been accomplished at that point: entered in, obeyed, received the Holy Ghost. The chapter's climax arrives here, one verse before it is declared insufficient.

verses.label: v. 19–21
verses.title: The question that reopens it
verses.text: The record raises its own objection and answers it in one word: "I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay." What follows is four requirements, press forward, have a perfect brightness of hope, love God and all men, and feast upon the word of Christ, ending in "endure to the end." Verse 21 then closes with an exclusivity claim in the same wording used at Mosiah 3:17, "there is none other way nor name given under heaven whereby man can be saved," and names the whole "the doctrine of Christ," a phrase used at verse 2, here, and at 3 Nephi 11:32–39.

chapter.title: The chapter's shape is its argument
chapter.text: Example, reasoning, revelation, conditions, gate, and then a question that reopens everything. A reader who stops at verse 18 has the ordinance without the life. Nephi builds the sequence carefully and then refuses to let it be the whole answer.

chapter.title: Discipleship is defined as imitation
chapter.text: Follow thou me, do the things ye have seen me do, follow your Lord and Savior down into the water, follow the example of the Son. The verb recurs throughout, and the chapter never describes belief without an accompanying action taken in the same order the Lord took it.

chapter.title: Nephi shows his work
chapter.text: Verse 16 marks the boundary between what the Father said and what Nephi concludes from it. In a chapter full of quoted revelation, that distinction is maintained, and it is a habit worth noticing in a writer who has just spent six chapters on prophecy.

chapter.title: Plainness is finally demonstrated
chapter.text: He claimed it in chapter 25 and practiced it in argument since. Here the subject is a procedure and the prose becomes procedural: numbered conditions, a sequence, a question, an answer. The style follows the subject, which is what he said plainness was for.

chapter.title: The three-verse ending carries the record's practical theology
chapter.text: Press forward, brightness of hope, love of God and of all men, feast on the word, endure. Later writers in this volume quote or echo these lines more than almost anything else Nephi writes, and they arrive as an answer to a question about whether the work is finished.

chapter.title: The unit begins here
chapter.text: Chapters 31 through 33 are Nephi's closing: the doctrine, its application, and his farewell. The commentary unit ended with Isaiah quoted; this one opens with Christ quoted, and the difference in pitch is the point of the division.

applications.title: Reason from the greater to the lesser
applications.text: Take something you know Christ did that you have excused yourself from, and run Nephi's argument: if he needed it, how much more do I. The chapter's whole case for baptism is built on that one move.

applications.title: Check the intent behind the act
applications.text: Pick one religious practice you keep faithfully and examine whether you bring real intent to it. The chapter's conditions are almost entirely about sincerity, and it lists three ways of faking before naming the real thing.

applications.title: Ask verse 19's question about yourself
applications.text: Whatever you have completed, whether a baptism, a covenant, a calling, or a repentance, ask whether you have been treating it as the finish. Nephi's answer is one word, and the three verses after it are what to do instead.

applications.title: Feast rather than read
applications.text: For one week, change the verb. Read scripture the way you eat a good meal: slowly, for pleasure, until full. The chapter puts feasting between pressing forward and enduring as the thing that makes both possible.

applications.title: Carry all four
applications.text: Steadfastness, brightness of hope, love of God, love of all men. Name which of the four is thinnest in you right now, and give it deliberate attention this month rather than working on the one that is already strong.

applications.title: Follow in order
applications.text: The instruction is to do the things you have seen him do. Choose one specific action from the gospels, not a disposition, and do that thing this week in the same order he did it: humble first, act second.

questions.text: What have I decided I do not need because I am already reasonably good?
When did I last humble myself before the Father in a way that someone could have observed?
Where is my outward act ahead of my inward aim?
What do I know by revelation, and what have I concluded on my own? Do I keep the two straight?
What am I treating as done?
Is my hope a perfect brightness or a cautious estimate, and what would change it?
